solution.why_others_wrong: 3 counts only the carboxylic acids and leaves out picric acid, a phenol with a pKa of 0.5; 5 includes 4-nitrophenol, which is still weaker than carbonic acid.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', acidity of carboxylic acids

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following alcohols give turbidity immediately with Lucas reagent (concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl₂) at room temperature?
2-Methylpropan-2-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylbutan-2-ol, propan-1-ol, 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol, cyclohexanol, butan-1-ol

solution.explanation: Tertiary alcohols form the insoluble alkyl chloride at once and give turbidity immediately; primary alcohols give no turbidity at room temperature (secondary alcohols react more slowly).
steps: Secondary: butan-2-ol, cyclohexanol; primary: propan-1-ol, butan-1-ol
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 or 2 misses the cyclic tertiary alcohol 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol or 2-methylbutan-2-ol; 5 adds the secondary alcohols, which do not react immediately.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', distinguishing primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the Reimer–Tiemann reaction, phenol is treated with chloroform in the presence of aqueous sodium hydroxide, and salicylaldehyde is obtained after acidification. The intermediate that is hydrolysed by the alkali in this reaction is:

solution.explanation: NCERT: a –CHO group is introduced at the ortho position of the benzene ring; an intermediate substituted benzal chloride (a –CHCl₂ group on the phenoxide ring) is hydrolysed in the presence of alkali to give salicylaldehyde.
solution.why_others_wrong: Benzoyl chloride (C₆H₅COCl) and benzyl chloride (C₆H₅CH₂Cl) carry the wrong number of chlorine atoms on the side chain; chlorobenzene has chlorine on the ring and cannot give an aldehyde group.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', Reimer–Tiemann reaction
solution.final_answer: Option D: A substituted benzal chloride

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Which reagent reduces carboxylic acids to primary alcohols but does not easily reduce functional groups such as ester, nitro and halo groups?

solution.explanation: NCERT: carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols by lithium aluminium hydride or, better, by diborane. Diborane does not easily reduce functional groups such as ester, nitro and halo. Sodium borohydride does not reduce the carboxyl group.
steps: Diborane: –COOH → –CH₂OH; leaves ester, nitro, halo largely untouched
solution.why_others_wrong: LiAlH₄ reduces esters as well; NaBH₄ does not reduce –COOH; Zn–Hg/HCl is used for Clemmensen reduction of aldehydes and ketones.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', reduction of carboxylic acids

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Ketones are readily oxidised by Tollens' reagent to carboxylic acids having the same number of carbon atoms.
Reason (R): In aldehydes, the hydrogen atom on the carbonyl carbon is converted into an –OH group on oxidation, without breaking any carbon–carbon bond.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Aldehydes are oxidised easily, even by mild oxidising agents such as Tollens' reagent, because of the H on the carbonyl carbon (R). Ketones lack this hydrogen; they are oxidised only under vigorous conditions by strong oxidising agents, with cleavage of C–C bonds, giving acids with fewer carbon atoms. A is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', oxidation of aldehydes and ketones
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Esters are reduced to aldehydes by diisobutylaluminium hydride (DIBAL-H).
Statement II: Propanone undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction when heated with concentrated NaOH.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT notes that DIBAL-H reduces nitriles to imines (then aldehydes on hydrolysis) and that esters are also reduced to aldehydes with DIBAL-H. The Cannizzaro reaction is shown by aldehydes with no α-hydrogen; propanone is a ketone with six α-hydrogens and instead undergoes aldol reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', preparation of aldehydes; Cannizzaro reaction
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
The vapours of each alcohol in List-I are passed over heated copper at 573 K. Match it with the main organic product in List-II.

List-I:
A. Ethanol
B. Propan-2-ol
C. 2-Methylpropan-2-ol
D. Methanol

List-II:
I. Methanal
II. 2-Methylpropene
III. Propanone
IV. Ethanal

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Over heated copper, primary alcohols are dehydrogenated to aldehydes and secondary alcohols to ketones. A tertiary alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon, so it is dehydrated to an alkene instead.
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes that give the tertiary alcohol a carbonyl product ignore the missing α-hydrogen on the carbinol carbon; codes that swap ethanol and propan-2-ol mix up aldehyde and ketone formation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', dehydrogenation of alcohols
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following give benzaldehyde as the main organic product?

(a) Toluene treated with chromyl chloride in CS₂, followed by hydrolysis
(b) Benzene treated with carbon monoxide and HCl in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃ or CuCl
(c) Benzoyl chloride hydrogenated over palladium on barium sulphate
(d) Benzonitrile reduced with SnCl₂ and HCl, followed by hydrolysis
(e) Toluene oxidised with alkaline KMnO₄, followed by acidification

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Etard reaction (chromyl chloride), Gattermann–Koch reaction (CO + HCl), Rosenmund reduction (H₂, Pd–BaSO₄) and Stephen reaction (SnCl₂/HCl, then H₃O⁺) all give benzaldehyde. Strong oxidation of toluene with KMnO₄ goes on to benzoic acid.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (e) forget that KMnO₄ oxidises the side chain right up to –COOH; (a), (b) and (c) only leaves out the Stephen reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', preparation of aldehydes

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Ethanol is oxidised to ethanoic acid by acidified potassium dichromate. The half-reactions are
Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O and C₂H₅OH + H₂O → CH₃COOH + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
The minimum mass of K₂Cr₂O₇ (molar mass 294 g mol⁻¹) needed to oxidise 4.6 g of ethanol completely is (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16):

solution.concept: Electron balance in the oxidation of an alcohol
solution.explanation: Equate the electrons lost by ethanol to the electrons gained by dichromate.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.8 g counts only 2 electrons per ethanol (oxidation stopping at ethanal); 29.4 g takes a 1 : 1 mole ratio; 14.7 g uses 3 electrons per ethanol.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', oxidation of alcohols

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 4.2 g of propene is converted into an alcohol by hydroboration–oxidation (B₂H₆, then H₂O₂/OH⁻). The alcohol is oxidised with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC), and the product is warmed with an excess of Tollens' reagent. Assuming every step is complete, the mass of silver deposited is (C = 12, H = 1, Ag = 108):

solution.concept: Regiochemistry of hydroboration and the Tollens' test
solution.explanation: Hydroboration–oxidation adds water in an anti-Markovnikov manner, giving propan-1-ol. PCC oxidises a primary alcohol only to the aldehyde, propanal, which reduces Tollens' reagent: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ + 3OH⁻ → RCOO⁻ + 2Ag + 2H₂O + 4NH₃.
steps: Propene: 4.2 / 42 = 0.10 mol → 0.10 mol propan-1-ol → 0.10 mol propanal
solution.why_others_wrong: 0 g assumes Markovnikov addition (propan-2-ol → propanone, which gives no silver mirror); 10.8 g uses one Ag per aldehyde; 43.2 g uses four, as for methanal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', hydroboration–oxidation; 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', Tollens' test

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When methyl tert-butyl ether, CH₃–O–C(CH₃)₃, is heated with HI, the products are methanol and 2-iodo-2-methylpropane.
Reason (R): In this cleavage, the iodide ion attacks the methyl carbon by the SN2 mechanism.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Cleavage of ethers containing a tertiary alkyl group
solution.explanation: When one alkyl group is tertiary, the protonated ether ionises by the SN1 mechanism to give the stable tert-butyl carbocation, which combines with I⁻; methanol is the other product. An SN2 attack on the methyl carbon would instead give CH₃I and tert-butyl alcohol. So A is true and R is false.
steps: R: false; the reaction follows SN1
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', cleavage of C–O bond in ethers
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid at 298 K to give p-nitrophenol as the only product.
Statement II: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is a weaker acid than phenol.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Nitration of phenol; acidity of nitrophenols
solution.explanation: With dilute HNO₃ at low temperature (298 K), phenol gives a mixture of ortho- and para-nitrophenols, which are separated by steam distillation. Three –NO₂ groups make picric acid a much stronger acid than phenol (pKa about 0.5 against 10.0).
steps: Statement I: false; o- and p-nitrophenols are formed
Statement II: false; picric acid is far stronger
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers', nitration of phenol; acidity of phenols
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following pairs can be distinguished by the test given?

(a) Propanal and propanone: Tollens' reagent
(b) Pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one: iodoform test (I₂ and NaOH)
(c) Benzaldehyde and acetophenone: Fehling's solution
(d) Phenol and benzoic acid: aqueous NaHCO₃
(e) Ethanol and methanol: 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Chemical tests that distinguish oxygen compounds
solution.explanation: Propanal reduces Tollens' reagent, propanone does not. Pentan-2-one is a methyl ketone and gives iodoform; pentan-3-one does not. Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde do not respond to Fehling's test, and acetophenone (a ketone) does not either, so Fehling's solution cannot tell them apart. Benzoic acid liberates CO₂ from NaHCO₃, phenol does not. Neither alcohol has a carbonyl group, so neither reacts with 2,4-DNP.
steps: (c) false: neither gives a positive Fehling's test
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (c) assume every aldehyde reduces Fehling's solution; options containing (e) use a carbonyl reagent on two alcohols.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', chemical tests to distinguish aldehydes and ketones

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the carbonyl group are correct?

(a) The carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised and lies at the centre of a trigonal planar arrangement, with bond angles of about 120°.
(b) The carbonyl carbon is an electrophilic (Lewis acid) centre and the carbonyl oxygen a nucleophilic (Lewis base) centre.
(c) Carbonyl compounds have substantial dipole moments and are more polar than ethers.
(d) The carboxylic carbon of a carboxylic acid is more electrophilic than the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde.
(e) The C=O bond of an aldehyde is non-polar, because both atoms share the π electrons equally.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT: the carbonyl carbon is sp² hybridised, trigonal planar, with ~120° bond angles; the C=O bond is polarised because oxygen is more electronegative, making carbon an electrophilic centre and oxygen a nucleophilic centre; carbonyl compounds have substantial dipole moments and are more polar than ethers. In carboxylic acids the carboxylic carbon is less electrophilic than the carbonyl carbon because of resonance with the –OH oxygen.
steps: (d) false: resonance makes it less electrophilic
(e) false: the C=O bond is polar
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) overlook the resonance of the carboxyl group; the option with (e) ignores the electronegativity difference between carbon and oxygen.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Aldehydes, Ketones and Carboxylic Acids', nature of carbonyl group; structure of carboxyl group

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In an arylamine, the nitrogen atom is bonded directly to a carbon atom of an aromatic ring. How many of the following are arylamines?
Aniline, benzylamine (C₆H₅CH₂NH₂), N-methylaniline, 4-methylaniline, cyclohexanamine, N,N-dimethylaniline, 2-phenylethanamine (C₆H₅CH₂CH₂NH₂)

solution.explanation: Only the position of nitrogen matters: it must be attached to the ring itself. Benzylamine and 2-phenylethanamine have the amino group on a side-chain carbon, so they are aliphatic amines; cyclohexanamine has no aromatic ring.
solution.why_others_wrong: Lower counts leave out the secondary and tertiary arylamines (N-methyl and N,N-dimethyl anilines); being 2° or 3° does not change the aryl classification.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', classification of amines

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: Ethanamine is soluble in water, whereas aniline is only sparingly soluble. The reason is that:

options.text: aniline is a stronger base than ethanamine
ethanamine forms hydrogen bonds with water, whereas the large hydrophobic C₆H₅ group of aniline decreases the extent of hydrogen bonding with water
the nitrogen atom of aniline has no lone pair of electrons

solution.explanation: Lower aliphatic amines dissolve in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. In aniline the large hydrocarbon (phenyl) part is hydrophobic, so the extent of hydrogen bonding, and hence the solubility, decreases.
steps: Both have –NH₂ able to hydrogen bond
Large hydrophobic C₆H₅ part in aniline → lower solubility
solution.why_others_wrong: Aniline is a weaker base than ethanamine; ethanamine is a covalent molecule; aniline's nitrogen does carry a lone pair, though it is partly delocalised into the ring.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', physical properties
solution.final_answer: Option B: ethanamine forms hydrogen bonds with water, whereas the large hydrophobic C₆H₅ group of aniline decreases the extent of hydrogen bonding with water

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In replacing the diazonium group by chlorine, the yield in the Sandmeyer reaction (CuCl/HCl) is better than in the Gattermann reaction (copper powder/HCl).
Statement II: If the temperature of a benzenediazonium chloride solution is allowed to rise up to 283 K, the salt is hydrolysed to phenol.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: NCERT: chloro and bromo groups can be introduced either with Cu(I) halides (Sandmeyer) or with copper powder and the halogen acid (Gattermann); the yield in the Sandmeyer reaction is found to be better. A diazonium salt solution warmed up to 283 K is hydrolysed to phenol.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', chemical reactions of diazonium salts
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the common name of the amine in List-I with its IUPAC name in List-II.

List-I:
A. Allylamine, CH₂=CH–CH₂–NH₂
B. Hexamethylenediamine, H₂N–(CH₂)₆–NH₂
C. Isopropylamine, (CH₃)₂CH–NH₂
D. Dimethylamine, (CH₃)₂NH

List-II:
I. N-Methylmethanamine
II. Propan-2-amine
III. Prop-2-en-1-amine
IV. Hexane-1,6-diamine

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Amines are named by replacing the 'e' of the alkane with 'amine' (keeping 'e' before 'diamine'); the position of –NH₂ is given by a locant; extra alkyl groups on nitrogen are shown with the prefix N-.
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping isopropylamine and dimethylamine confuses a 1° amine with a 2° amine; swapping the first two pairs a C₃ unsaturated amine with a C₆ diamine.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', nomenclature
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: 1,3,5-Tribromobenzene cannot be made by direct bromination of benzene but can be made from aniline. 3.30 g of 2,4,6-tribromoaniline is diazotised at 273–278 K, and the diazonium salt is treated with hypophosphorous acid (H₃PO₂). Assuming every step is complete, the mass of 1,3,5-tribromobenzene formed is (C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, Br = 80):

solution.explanation: Hypophosphorous acid reduces the diazonium salt and replaces –N₂⁺ by –H, so the three bromine atoms are left in the 1,3,5 positions, which direct bromination of benzene cannot give.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.30 g repeats the mass of the amine; 2.36 g is for a dibromobenzene; 6.30 g doubles the moles.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', importance of diazonium salts in synthesis of aromatic compounds

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
How many of the following give a diazonium salt that is stable enough to be used in solution at 273–278 K when treated with NaNO₂ and dilute HCl?
Aniline, 4-methylaniline, 4-nitroaniline, benzylamine, ethanamine, N-methylaniline

solution.explanation: Only primary aromatic amines form arenediazonium salts, which are stable for a short time at low temperature. Primary aliphatic amines (including benzylamine, where –NH₂ is on a side chain) give unstable aliphatic diazonium salts that decompose at once with evolution of N₂. A secondary amine such as N-methylaniline has only one H on nitrogen and cannot form a diazonium salt.
steps: Benzylamine, ethanamine: primary aliphatic; N-methylaniline: secondary
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 includes benzylamine, whose nitrogen is not on the ring; 2 leaves out 4-nitroaniline, which is still a primary aromatic amine.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', reaction with nitrous acid; diazonium salts

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): N,N-Dimethylaniline reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride to give a sulphonamide that is insoluble in aqueous alkali.
Reason (R): Tertiary amines have no hydrogen atom on the nitrogen atom.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: Benzenesulphonyl chloride replaces a hydrogen atom on nitrogen. N,N-Dimethylaniline is a tertiary amine with no N–H, so it does not react with Hinsberg's reagent at all; an alkali-insoluble sulphonamide is characteristic of secondary amines. A is false, R is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', reaction with arylsulphonyl chloride
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Secondary amines react with benzenesulphonyl chloride to give a sulphonamide that dissolves in aqueous alkali.
Statement II: Primary aromatic amines react with nitrous acid at 273–278 K to form arenediazonium salts.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: The N,N-dialkylbenzenesulphonamide from a secondary amine has no hydrogen on nitrogen and so is not acidic; it is insoluble in alkali (the alkali-soluble product comes from a primary amine). Primary aromatic amines give arenediazonium salts with nitrous acid in the cold.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', chemical reactions: Hinsberg's test; reaction with nitrous acid
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The correct order of basic strength in aqueous solution is:

solution.concept: Effect of substituents on the basicity of aniline
solution.explanation: Electron-releasing groups such as –CH₃ increase the electron density on nitrogen and raise the basic strength; electron-withdrawing groups such as –NO₂ lower it.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other orders either ignore the activating effect of –CH₃ or treat –NO₂ as electron releasing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', basic character of arylamines

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: The pKb of aniline is 9.38. Treating aniline as a weak base that is only slightly ionised, the pH of a 0.10 M aqueous solution of aniline at 298 K is (pKw = 14.00):

solution.concept: pH of a solution of a weak base
solution.explanation: For a weak base, [OH⁻] = √(Kb·C), so pOH = ½(pKb − log C).
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.19 is the pOH, not the pH; 4.62 is 14 − 9.38, which treats pKb as pOH; 9.38 is simply the pKb.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', basic character of amines (pKb values)

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: An amine X, C₃H₉N, reacts with benzenesulphonyl chloride to give a product that is insoluble in aqueous alkali, and it does not give the carbylamine test. X is:

solution.concept: Identifying an amine by Hinsberg's and carbylamine tests
solution.explanation: An alkali-insoluble Hinsberg product is given by a secondary amine. The carbylamine test is given only by primary amines, so a negative result is consistent. The only secondary amine of formula C₃H₉N is CH₃–NH–C₂H₅.
solution.why_others_wrong: Propan-1-amine and propan-2-amine are primary (alkali-soluble product, positive carbylamine test); trimethylamine (N,N-dimethylmethanamine) does not react with benzenesulphonyl chloride.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', identification of primary, secondary and tertiary amines

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): 4-Nitroaniline is a much weaker base than aniline.
Reason (R): The –NO₂ group at the para position withdraws electron density from the nitrogen lone pair by its −R and −I effects, making the lone pair less available for protonation.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Electron-withdrawing groups and the basicity of arylamines
solution.explanation: In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is already partly delocalised into the ring. A para –NO₂ group pulls this electron density further, through the ring onto itself (−R) and through σ bonds (−I), so protonation is much less favourable. R gives the reason for A.
steps: R: true and the cause of A
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', basic character of arylamines
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Consider three amines: X = ethanamine, Y = aniline and Z = N-methylaniline. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) X and Y both give a foul-smelling isocyanide when warmed with chloroform and ethanolic KOH.
(b) Y, after treatment with NaNO₂ and dilute HCl at 273–278 K, gives a coloured azo dye with an alkaline solution of phenol.
(c) Z gives a product with benzenesulphonyl chloride that is insoluble in aqueous alkali.
(d) X gives a diazonium salt that is stable in solution at 273–278 K.
(e) Z gives the carbylamine test.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Distinguishing primary aliphatic, primary aromatic and secondary amines
solution.explanation: The carbylamine test is given by primary amines, aliphatic and aromatic. Only primary aromatic amines give stable diazonium salts, which couple with phenol to give azo dyes; ethanamine's diazonium salt decomposes at once, releasing N₂. N-Methylaniline, a secondary amine, gives an alkali-insoluble sulphonamide and no isocyanide.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) forget that aliphatic diazonium salts are unstable; options with (e) apply the carbylamine test to a secondary amine.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Amines', chemical reactions; diazonium salts

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: According to NCERT, amylose is a long unbranched chain of α-D-(+)-glucose units held together by C1–C4 glycosidic linkages. The number of glucose units in such a chain is about:

solution.explanation: Amylose, the water-soluble component (15–20%) of starch, is a long unbranched chain of 200–1000 α-D-(+)-glucose units joined by C1–C4 glycosidic linkages.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 to 10 units defines an oligosaccharide; 20 to 50 and 50,000 to 100,000 are not the figures NCERT gives for amylose.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', polysaccharides: starch

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the vitamin in List-I with its sources, as given in NCERT, in List-II.

List-I:
A. Vitamin A
B. Vitamin B₁ (thiamine)
C. Vitamin B₂ (riboflavin)
D. Vitamin K

List-II:
I. Green leafy vegetables
II. Milk, egg white, liver, kidney
III. Fish liver oil, carrots, butter and milk
IV. Yeast, milk, green vegetables and cereals

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: NCERT's table of vitamins lists: A — fish liver oil, carrots, butter and milk; B₁ — yeast, milk, green vegetables and cereals; B₂ — milk, egg white, liver, kidney; K — green leafy vegetables.
solution.why_others_wrong: Codes that swap B₁ and B₂ or A and B₁ mix up two lists that both contain milk; the last code gives vitamin K the animal sources of riboflavin.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', vitamins: sources and deficiency diseases
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the zwitter ionic form, amino acids show amphoteric behaviour, as they react with both acids and bases.
Statement II: Most naturally occurring α-amino acids have the L-configuration.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: In water the –COOH group loses a proton and the –NH₂ group gains one, giving a dipolar ion (zwitterion). It can accept a proton (acting as a base) through –COO⁻ or give one (acting as an acid) through –NH₃⁺. All naturally occurring α-amino acids except glycine are optically active, and most of them have the L-configuration.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', amino acids: properties
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Sucrose reduces Tollens' reagent.
Reason (R): On hydrolysis, sucrose gives glucose and fructose.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: In sucrose, C1 of α-D-glucose is joined to C2 of β-D-fructose, so the reducing groups of both units are used up in the glycosidic bond; sucrose is a non-reducing sugar and does not reduce Tollens' reagent. R is a true statement about its hydrolysis (to invert sugar). A is false.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', disaccharides: sucrose
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In a nucleic acid strand, successive nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester linkages between the 5′ and 3′ carbon atoms of their pentose sugars. How many phosphodiester linkages are present in a linear, double-stranded DNA segment of 50 base pairs?

solution.explanation: A linear strand of n nucleotides has n − 1 linkages between neighbouring nucleotides. A double-stranded segment of 50 base pairs has two strands of 50 nucleotides each. Base pairing between the strands is by hydrogen bonds, not phosphodiester linkages.
solution.why_others_wrong: 49 counts only one strand; 50 and 100 count one linkage per nucleotide, which would be true only for a circular strand.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', structure of nucleic acids

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the dipeptide glycylalanine (Gly–Ala), the carboxyl group of glycine is joined to the amino group of alanine. By the same convention, in the tripeptide Gly–Ala–Val, the amino acid residue that carries the free α-amino (–NH₂) group is:

options.text: None; all the α-amino groups are used in peptide bonds

solution.explanation: In Gly–Ala–Val, the –COOH of glycine forms a peptide bond with the –NH₂ of alanine, and the –COOH of alanine with the –NH₂ of valine. The –NH₂ of glycine remains free, and the –COOH of valine remains free.
solution.why_others_wrong: Alanine's amino group and valine's amino group are both used in peptide bonds; a linear peptide always keeps one free amino group at one end.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', proteins: peptide bond

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A protein loses its biological activity on denaturation.
Reason (R): During denaturation, the secondary and tertiary structures of the protein are destroyed, although its primary structure remains intact.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.explanation: A native protein owes its biological activity to its unique three-dimensional structure. A change in temperature or pH disturbs the hydrogen bonds; the globules unfold and the helix uncoils, destroying the secondary and tertiary structures, and the protein loses its biological activity. R explains A.
steps: Activity depends on the 3-D (2° and 3°) structure
Denaturation destroys 2° and 3° structure → activity lost
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', denaturation of proteins
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Glycogen is less highly branched than amylopectin.
Statement II: Cellulose is a straight-chain polysaccharide made of α-D-glucose units.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Glycogen, the animal starch, has a structure similar to amylopectin but is more highly branched. Cellulose is a straight-chain polysaccharide made only of β-D-glucose units, joined by glycosidic linkages between C1 of one unit and C4 of the next.
steps: Statement I: false (glycogen is more branched)
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', polysaccharides: cellulose and glycogen
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about nucleic acids are correct?

(a) Nucleic acids are long-chain polymers of nucleotides and are therefore also called polynucleotides.
(b) The sugar in DNA is β-D-2-deoxyribose, whereas the sugar in RNA is β-D-ribose.
(c) Cytosine is present in both DNA and RNA.
(d) In a nucleotide, the phosphoric acid is linked to the 1′ position of the pentose sugar.
(e) A nucleoside contains a base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Nucleic acids are polynucleotides. DNA contains β-D-2-deoxyribose and RNA β-D-ribose; cytosine and the two purines occur in both, while thymine is only in DNA and uracil only in RNA. The base is attached at C-1′ of the sugar (nucleoside); the phosphoric acid is esterified at C-5′ (nucleotide).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) put the phosphate where the base is attached; options with (e) confuse a nucleoside with a nucleotide.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', chemical composition and structure of nucleic acids

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: A linear double-stranded DNA molecule contains 1000 nucleotides, of which 22% are guanine. An A–T pair is held by two hydrogen bonds and a G–C pair by three. The total number of hydrogen bonds between the two strands is:

solution.explanation: In double-stranded DNA, G pairs with C and A with T, so the number of G–C pairs equals the number of G nucleotides. 1000 nucleotides make 500 base pairs.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1280 swaps the numbers of A–T and G–C pairs; 1110 takes 22% of the 500 pairs as G–C pairs; 1500 assumes three hydrogen bonds for every pair.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', structure of DNA

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the carbohydrate in List-I with the product(s) of its complete hydrolysis in List-II.

List-I:
A. Sucrose
B. Lactose
C. Cellulose
D. Amylose

List-II:
I. α-D-Glucose only
II. D-Glucose and D-galactose
III. D-Glucose and D-fructose
IV. β-D-Glucose only

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Monosaccharide units of di- and polysaccharides
solution.explanation: Sucrose is made of α-D-glucose and β-D-fructose; lactose of β-D-galactose and β-D-glucose; cellulose only of β-D-glucose units; amylose only of α-D-glucose units.
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping cellulose and amylose confuses the α and β linkages of starch and cellulose; swapping sucrose and lactose mixes up fructose and galactose.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', disaccharides and polysaccharides
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following conclusions about the structure of glucose are correctly drawn from the observation stated?

(a) Glucose forms a pentaacetate with acetic anhydride, so it contains five –OH groups.
(b) Prolonged heating with HI gives n-hexane, so the six carbon atoms are linked in a straight chain.
(c) Glucose exists in two crystalline forms, α and β, which the open-chain structure cannot explain.
(d) α-D-Glucose and β-D-glucose differ in the configuration at C-5.
(e) Bromine water oxidises glucose to gluconic acid, so glucose contains a ketonic carbonyl group.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Evidence for the structure of glucose
solution.explanation: Acetylation to a pentaacetate shows five –OH groups; reduction to n-hexane shows a straight six-carbon chain; the α and β forms (anomers) need the cyclic hemiacetal structure. The anomers differ at C-1, the anomeric carbon. Oxidation by the mild oxidant bromine water to gluconic acid, a six-carbon acid, shows an aldehyde group.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) put the anomeric difference at the ring-closing carbon C-5; options with (e) reverse the meaning of the bromine water test.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', structure of glucose

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the structure of proteins are correct?

(a) The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids, and any change in this sequence creates a different protein.
(b) Quaternary structure is found only in proteins made up of two or more polypeptide chains (subunits).
(c) Denaturation of a protein hydrolyses its peptide bonds.
(d) In the α-helix, the –NH group of each amino acid residue is hydrogen bonded to the >C=O of an adjacent turn of the helix.
(e) Globular proteins such as insulin are usually insoluble in water.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Primary structure = amino acid sequence; changing it gives a different protein. Quaternary structure is the spatial arrangement of two or more subunits. In the α-helix, the chain twists into a right-handed screw with –NH···O=C hydrogen bonds between successive turns. Denaturation destroys 2° and 3° structure but leaves the peptide bonds (primary structure) intact. Globular proteins are usually water soluble.
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) treat denaturation as hydrolysis; the option with (e) gives globular proteins the solubility of fibrous ones.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Chemistry, 'Biomolecules', structure of proteins

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In the laboratory, sols are prepared of the following substances. How many of them form lyophilic sols?
Starch, gum, egg albumin, ferric hydroxide, arsenious sulphide, aluminium hydroxide

solution.explanation: Lyophilic sols are formed directly by warming and stirring substances such as starch, gum and egg albumin with water. Ferric hydroxide, aluminium hydroxide and arsenious sulphide give lyophobic sols, which need special methods (hydrolysis, double decomposition).
solution.why_others_wrong: Counts of 1 or 2 miss gum or egg albumin; 4 counts a metal hydroxide sol, which is lyophobic.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), preparation of lyophilic and lyophobic sols

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the laboratory, a lyophobic sol of arsenious sulphide, As₂S₃, is prepared by:

options.text: adding iron(III) chloride solution drop by drop to boiling water
passing hydrogen sulphide gas through a dilute aqueous solution of arsenious oxide
warming arsenious oxide with water and stirring well
adding sodium hydroxide solution to aluminium sulphate solution

solution.concept: Preparation of a lyophobic sol by double decomposition
solution.explanation: Arsenious sulphide sol is made by a chemical reaction: H₂S is passed through a dilute solution of As₂O₃ in water, As₂O₃ + 3H₂S → As₂S₃ (sol) + 3H₂O.
solution.why_others_wrong: FeCl₃ in boiling water gives a ferric hydroxide sol; simply warming and stirring works only for lyophilic substances; NaOH with aluminium sulphate gives a precipitate of Al(OH)₃.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), preparation of lyophobic sols
solution.final_answer: Option B: passing hydrogen sulphide gas through a dilute aqueous solution of arsenious oxide

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution and pink in alkaline solution.
Statement II: Methyl orange is red in acidic solution and yellow in alkaline solution.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and turns pink in alkali; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali. These colour changes are used to detect the end points of acid–base titrations.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), titrimetric analysis: indicators
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
In salt analysis, a little of each salt is warmed with dilute H₂SO₄. How many of the following anions give a gas under these conditions?
CO₃²⁻, S²⁻, NO₂⁻, SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻

solution.concept: Dilute sulphuric acid group of anions
solution.explanation: Carbonate gives CO₂ (turns lime water milky), sulphide gives H₂S (turns lead acetate paper black) and nitrite gives brown fumes of NO₂ with dilute H₂SO₄. Nitrate, chloride, bromide and iodide react only with concentrated H₂SO₄; sulphate does not react.
steps: Dilute H₂SO₄ group: CO₃²⁻, S²⁻, NO₂⁻ → 3
Concentrated H₂SO₄ group: NO₃⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻; SO₄²⁻: neither
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 usually forgets the nitrite ion; 4 or 5 add halides or nitrate, which need concentrated H₂SO₄.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), qualitative analysis: tests for anions

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text: In the test for NH₄⁺, 0.535 g of ammonium chloride is heated with an excess of NaOH solution, and all the ammonia evolved is absorbed in 0.10 M HCl. The volume of the acid exactly neutralised is (N = 14, H = 1, Cl = 35.5):

solution.explanation: NH₄Cl + NaOH → NaCl + NH₃ + H₂O; NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl. One mole of ammonium chloride gives one mole of NH₃, which neutralises one mole of HCl.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 mL halves the ammonia; 200 mL doubles it; 10 mL uses the molarity as 1.0 M.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), qualitative analysis: test for ammonium ion

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide in acidic solution at room temperature, the rate increases when the concentration of iodide ions is increased.
Statement II: The rate of this reaction does not depend on the concentration of hydrogen peroxide.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Kinetics of the iodide–hydrogen peroxide reaction
solution.explanation: The reaction H₂O₂ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → I₂ + 2H₂O follows the rate law rate = k[H₂O₂][I⁻] under the experimental conditions, so the rate rises with an increase in the concentration of either reactant.
steps: Statement II: false; first order in H₂O₂
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), chemical kinetics: reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Match the compound prepared in the laboratory (List-I) with the starting materials used (List-II).

List-I:
A. Mohr's salt
B. Potash alum
C. p-Nitroacetanilide
D. Iodoform

List-II:
I. Acetanilide, with a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄
II. Ethanol or acetone, warmed with iodine and alkali
III. Iron(II) sulphate and ammonium sulphate, with a little dilute H₂SO₄
IV. Potassium sulphate and aluminium sulphate

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.explanation: Mohr's salt crystallises from an equimolar solution of FeSO₄ and (NH₄)₂SO₄ (dilute H₂SO₄ prevents hydrolysis); potash alum from K₂SO₄ and Al₂(SO₄)₃; p-nitroacetanilide by nitrating acetanilide; iodoform by the haloform reaction of ethanol or acetone with iodine and alkali.
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping Mohr's salt and potash alum confuses the two double sulphates; swapping p-nitroacetanilide and iodoform pairs a nitration with a haloform reaction.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), preparation of inorganic and organic compounds
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
The initial rate of the reaction H₂O₂ + 2I⁻ + 2H⁺ → I₂ + 2H₂O was measured at room temperature at a fixed, excess acidity:
Experiment 1: [H₂O₂] = 0.010 M, [I⁻] = 0.020 M, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
Experiment 2: [H₂O₂] = 0.020 M, [I⁻] = 0.020 M, rate = 4.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
Experiment 3: [H₂O₂] = 0.020 M, [I⁻] = 0.040 M, rate = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
The rate constant of the reaction is:

solution.concept: Finding orders and the rate constant from initial rates
solution.explanation: Compare experiments in which only one concentration changes to find each order, then substitute any one experiment into the rate law.
steps: Exp 1 → 2: [H₂O₂] doubled, rate doubled → first order in H₂O₂
Exp 2 → 3: [I⁻] doubled, rate doubled → first order in I⁻
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ and 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ treat the reaction as first order overall in one reactant only; 5.0 × 10⁻¹ L² mol⁻² s⁻¹ assumes second order in iodide.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), chemical kinetics: reaction of iodide ions with hydrogen peroxide

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Zn²⁺ is precipitated as ZnS when H₂S is passed through its ammoniacal solution, but not when H₂S is passed through its solution acidified with dilute HCl.
Reason (R): In ammoniacal solution the ionisation of H₂S increases, so the sulphide ion concentration becomes high enough for the ionic product of ZnS to exceed its solubility product.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Group separation by control of sulphide ion concentration
solution.explanation: H₂S ⇌ 2H⁺ + S²⁻. In dilute HCl the common ion H⁺ suppresses ionisation, and [S²⁻] is so low that only sulphides with very low Ksp (group II) precipitate. NH₄OH removes H⁺, increasing ionisation and [S²⁻], so ZnS (higher Ksp, group IV) precipitates. R explains A.
steps: Acidic: low [S²⁻] → ionic product of ZnS < Ksp
Ammoniacal: high [S²⁻] → ionic product > Ksp → ZnS
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), qualitative analysis of cations: group IV
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question_text:
The enthalpy of neutralisation of hydrochloric acid by sodium hydroxide is determined by mixing equal volumes of the two solutions, of the same molarity, in a calorimeter. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Using 1.0 M solutions instead of 0.5 M solutions (same volumes) gives a larger rise in temperature.
(b) Using half the volumes of the same solutions gives about half the rise in temperature.
(c) The heat capacity of the calorimeter must be taken into account to get an accurate value.
(d) Per mole of water formed, about the same value is obtained if nitric acid is used instead of hydrochloric acid.
(e) The enthalpy of neutralisation of ethanoic acid by NaOH is more negative than that of HCl by NaOH.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Calorimetric determination of the enthalpy of neutralisation
solution.explanation: Doubling the concentrations doubles the heat released into the same mass of solution, so ΔT is larger. Halving both volumes halves both the heat released and the mass to be heated, so ΔT stays about the same (ignoring the calorimeter). Part of the heat warms the calorimeter, so its heat capacity is needed. Any strong acid with a strong base gives about −57 kJ per mole of water. A weak acid such as ethanoic acid gives a less negative value, because some heat is used to ionise it.
steps: (b) false: ΔT is about the same
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (b) forget that the mass of solution is halved along with the heat; options with (e) reverse the weak-acid effect.
solution.ncert_reference: NCERT Laboratory Manual Chemistry (Class 11/12), thermochemistry: enthalpy of neutralisation
